problemText: Draft position for an argument essay: "This essay will discuss whether the town should build a new public library." Which revision best sharpens this into a defensible, arguable position?
choices: This essay will explore several differing perspectives on the town's ongoing library debate and let readers form their own conclusions.
Building a new public library would probably be a fairly nice, welcome addition for most residents of the town.
The town should fund a new central library because the current cramped hours already turn away working parents and students most evenings.
The town council has spent well over a decade debating possible new library locations, budgets, and staffing plans without ever reaching a final consensus on any of them.
hints: A defensible position commits to a specific stance, not a plan to 'discuss' or 'explore' a topic.
Ask whether a reasonable person could actually disagree with the sentence — if not, it's a fact or a topic, not a claim.

problemText: Draft position: "Homework is bad for students and should basically be eliminated." Which revision best sharpens this into a defensible, specific position that survives a genuine counter-position?
choices: Middle schools should cap nightly homework at thirty minutes per class because current loads leave too little time for sleep.
Homework has been an accepted, unquestioned part of American classrooms for a very long time now.
Homework is honestly just not very fun for most students most of the time, and plenty of them would rather be doing almost anything else.
Some people think homework is good and some people think homework is bad, and both sides have a point.
hints: A vague feeling ('not fun') isn't a claim a reader can push back against with specifics.
Look for the option that commits to a concrete, narrowed policy a reasonable person could actually oppose.

problemText: Claim: "Local high schools should require a semester of community-service volunteering before graduation." Draft paragraph: "Volunteering is a good experience. It helps students grow. Many students say they liked it." Which revision adds the most relevant, sufficient evidence to support the claim?
choices: Volunteering in some form has existed for centuries, tracing back to ancient charitable and religious traditions.
Most students probably feel rather differently about volunteering depending on their own personality, interests, family schedule, and how much free time they actually have.
Community service can mean many different things depending on which organization a student ends up joining.
A three-year study of a nearby district found a 22% rise in civic engagement among students who completed a required service semester.
hints: Relevant evidence bears on the specific claim (requiring a semester of service), not just the general topic of volunteering.
A vague statement about how students 'might feel' isn't evidence — look for a concrete, measurable finding.

problemText: Draft paragraph: "Later school start times help students. Also, sleep experts recommend them. Also, one district saw better attendance after switching. Later start times are clearly beneficial." Which revision best fixes this evidence-dump paragraph by sequencing it deliberately and adding commentary that connects each piece to the claim?
choices: Later start times help students, and also sleep experts recommend them, and also most teachers seem to support the idea, and also many parents say they like it as well.
Pediatric sleep experts recommend an 8:30 a.m. start because adolescent circadian rhythms shift; a nearby district that adopted this saw attendance rise the next year.
Later start times help students, a topic many school boards across the country have debated for years.
Sleep experts recommend later starts, students seem to like later starts, and attendance improved somewhere once, so later starts are good.
hints: An evidence dump strings pieces together with 'also' and no explanation of why one leads to the next.
Look for the option that explains WHY the authority's recommendation matters and HOW the district result corroborates it.

problemText: An essay argues cities should build more protected bike lanes. Three body-paragraph points are ready: (1) fewer collisions where protected lanes exist, (2) more foot traffic to small businesses on those streets, (3) construction cost concerns are real but manageable. Which revision states these as a coherent line of reasoning rather than a list of topics?
choices: This essay will discuss safety, then business impact, then construction cost, in whatever particular order happens to seem convenient to the writer at the time of drafting, without any particular reason for that order.
Cities should build bike lanes because lanes are about safety, lanes are about business, and lanes are about cost.
Because protected lanes measurably reduce collisions, and that same safety gain also draws more foot traffic to local businesses, cities should expand them.
Protected bike lanes involve safety considerations, business considerations, and cost considerations, each one worth thinking about separately.
hints: A line of reasoning shows each point building on or extending the one before it, not just naming three separate topics.
Apply the swap test: could these points trade places with nothing lost? If so, it's a list, not a reasoned sequence.

problemText: A student explains an essay's structure this way: "First I talk about safety, then business benefits, then cost. Each paragraph is about a different topic." Which revision most improves this into an actual statement of line of reasoning rather than a topic list?
choices: First I talk about safety, then business, then cost, because that's simply the order I thought of them.
I cover safety first, business second, and cost third, and honestly all three paragraphs matter about equally to the overall essay in the end.
My essay is organized into three parts — a safety part, a business part, a cost part — in logical order.
Establishing that lanes reduce collisions first gives the safety case standing before the business point extends it, and only then does cost answer the objection looming over both.
hints: Naming what each paragraph is 'about' describes a topic list, not a line of reasoning.
Look for the option that explains WHY the second point depends on the first, and why the third comes last.

problemText: Draft paragraph: "Some people might complain about the new curfew law, but they're wrong and the benefits clearly outweigh whatever they're worried about." Which revision best names and concedes a real objection, then rebuts it, instead of dismissing an unnamed one?
choices: Curfew opponents raise a real concern: the law could restrict teens who work evening shifts. That cost is genuine, but the ordinance exempts documented working students.
Critics of the curfew are simply misinformed and clearly haven't looked closely at the supporting data.
A few residents dislike the curfew, but most people in town seem to support it overall, so their complaints probably don't matter all that much.
The curfew law has been debated in city council meetings for several months without full agreement.
hints: A real counterargument names the strongest specific objection — not a vague 'some people complain.'
Look for the option that grants a true cost is real before explaining why the policy still handles it.

problemText: Draft paragraph addressing the objection that a proposed soda tax burdens low-income shoppers most: "That's true, low-income families would definitely be hurt the most by this tax, so maybe the tax isn't such a good idea after all." Which revision best concedes the true cost and then rebuts it, without abandoning the original claim?
choices: Low-income families are affected by all kinds of taxes, so this really isn't anything new to worry about.
It's true low-income households spend more on sugary drinks; the city can offset that by directing tax revenue toward produce vouchers for the same households.
That's a fair point, and honestly it might be reason enough to just drop the proposal.
People who oppose the soda tax are usually just opposed to any and all forms of government regulation, no matter what it happens to be regulating or how it's designed.
hints: The draft concedes the cost but then abandons the claim entirely — a rebuttal has to answer the objection, not surrender to it.
Look for the option that grants the real cost AND names a specific way the position still holds.

problemText: Draft opening line for an essay arguing a city should expand its public transit hours: "Throughout history, cities have had to make decisions about public transportation." Which revision most effectively opens the argument by establishing concrete stakes before stating the claim?
choices: Public transportation is an important topic that affects a great many people in many different ways.
Since the dawn of urban civilization, people have needed ways to move from place to place.
Every weeknight at 11:45, the last bus leaves the hospital stop, stranding overnight-shift nurses with no way home but an expensive cab ride.
This essay will discuss, in a fairly general and even-handed way, the various pros and cons of extending the city's public transit hours.
hints: A strong opening earns the claim with a concrete, specific scenario or detail — not a broad 'throughout history' frame.
Avoid the 'dictionary opening' and the sentence that just announces the essay's topic.

problemText: Draft conclusion: "In conclusion, as I have shown, the city should expand public transit hours because of the reasons discussed above." Which revision most effectively closes the argument by answering "so what" instead of restating the thesis?
choices: A nurse who no longer must choose between a shift and a safe ride home is one measure of a city that works for everyone.
In summary, expanding transit hours is something the city should clearly do for all of the reasons already given above in this essay in considerable detail.
As stated earlier, transit hours matter, and the reasons given above already make that clear.
To conclude, this essay has shown that public transit is important and hours should be extended.
hints: A strong conclusion projects the claim's significance forward instead of repeating the thesis in the same words.
Test: if you deleted the conclusion, would the essay feel unfinished, or would nothing be lost?

problemText: Draft position: "Social media has changed the way teenagers interact with each other, and this shift deserves closer examination by researchers and educators alike." Which revision best sharpens this into a defensible, specific position a reader could actually push back against?
choices: Schools should require a semester-long digital-literacy course because teenagers report struggling to recognize manipulative design patterns in the apps they use daily
Social media is a defining and pervasive feature of teenage life today, for better and for worse, in ways that likely differ considerably from one platform or community to the next
This paper will examine several distinct ways in which social media might be reshaping teenage social interaction, friendship formation, and self-image across different contexts
Many researchers, educators, and parent advocacy groups have expressed some degree of interest in formally studying how social media affects teenagers' daily behavior
hints: A defensible position commits to a specific proposal, not a general observation that something 'deserves examination.'
Ask which option a reasonable school board member could actually vote against.

problemText: Draft position: "The city's noise ordinance limiting outdoor events after 10 p.m. has led to disagreement between residents and nightlife business owners." Which revision most sharpens this into the writer's OWN defensible position, rather than a description of the dispute itself?
choices: The city's noise ordinance has led to disagreement between residents who want quiet nights and business owners who rely on late revenue, and both sides raise concerns worth taking seriously
Whether the city's noise ordinance is fair depends heavily on which neighborhood a given resident happens to live closest to
The city should replace its blanket 10 p.m. cutoff with a sliding curfew tied to each block's own measured noise levels, collected by the city's existing sensor network
The noise ordinance debate raises broader questions about how growing cities balance residential comfort against nightlife-driven economic vitality
hints: Naming that two sides disagree, or that fairness 'depends,' is not the same as the writer taking a position.
Look for the option that commits to a specific policy change the writer is arguing for.

problemText: Claim: "The city should install more crosswalk signals near the elementary school." Draft paragraph: "Crosswalks are important. Kids need to get to school safely. Many people think safety matters." Which revision adds the most relevant, sufficient evidence to support the claim?
choices: Crosswalk signals of one form or another have existed in American cities for well over a century now
A city traffic study recorded fourteen near-miss incidents at the school's unsignaled crossing in a single semester
Some neighborhoods happen to have more crosswalks installed than others depending on their overall physical size and layout
Most drivers say they generally try their best to watch out for pedestrians whenever possible
hints: Relevant evidence bears on the specific claim (this school's crossing), not the general history of crosswalks.
Look for a concrete, measurable finding rather than a vague impression of how people 'try' to behave.

problemText: Claim: "The library's new noise-free study room has improved students' ability to concentrate." Four possible sentences are under consideration for the evidence paragraph. Which one is both relevant to the claim AND sufficient on its own to support it, rather than merely on-topic?
choices: A single student mentioned in a brief hallway conversation, in passing, that the new room "seemed pretty quiet" to them
The room's construction was funded through a combination of PTA fundraising drives and a competitive state library grant
The room includes four enclosed study carrels, soundproofed walls, and seating for up to twelve students at a time
A schoolwide survey of every enrolled student found their average self-reported focus score rose from 5.8 to 7.4 after the room opened
hints: Funding source and room dimensions are true facts about the room, but neither speaks to concentration.
A single overheard comment is relevant but too thin to carry a claim alone — compare it to a measured, schoolwide result.

problemText: An essay argues cities should invest in urban tree planting. Three body-paragraph points are ready: (1) trees reduce summer temperatures in paved areas, (2) lower temperatures cut residents' summer cooling costs, (3) the planting program's cost is manageable within existing budgets. Which revision states these as a coherent line of reasoning rather than a list of topics?
choices: This essay will discuss temperature, then cost, then energy bills, in an order that could easily be rearranged without changing anything about the essay's overall meaning or its underlying persuasive force
Cities should plant trees because trees are about temperature, and trees are also about cost, and trees are also about energy in some general sense
Because trees measurably lower pavement temperatures, and that cooling effect directly reduces nearby residents' summer energy bills, cities can afford to expand tree planting
Urban tree planting involves temperature considerations, cost considerations, and energy considerations, each one worth exploring separately in its own right
hints: A line of reasoning shows one point building on the one before it, not three topics named side by side.
Apply the swap test: could these points trade places with nothing lost? If so, it's a list, not a reasoned sequence.

problemText: A student explains an essay's structure this way: "First I cover temperature, then energy costs, then program cost, because that's simply the order the notes happened to be arranged in." Which revision most improves this into an actual statement of line of reasoning rather than a topic list?
choices: Establishing that trees cool pavement first gives the energy-savings claim a mechanism to point to, and only then does program cost answer the objection either point might raise on its own
First I cover temperature, then energy costs, then program cost, and each of the three parts matters about equally to the overall persuasiveness of the finished essay
My essay is organized into three separate parts — a temperature part, an energy part, and a cost part — arranged in a logical and sensible order
First I cover temperature, then energy costs, then program cost, because that's simply the order the notes happened to be arranged in when I first drafted them
hints: Naming an order as 'logical' without explaining why one point depends on the last is still a topic list.
Look for the option that explains WHY the second point needs the first, and what the third point is answering.

problemText: Draft paragraph: "Some people might not like the new recycling fee, but they're wrong to complain since the city needs the revenue." Which revision best names and concedes a real objection, then rebuts it, instead of dismissing an unnamed one?
choices: Critics of the fee simply don't understand how municipal budgets and public works financing actually work in practice

A few residents dislike the fee, but most residents across the city support it overall, so their scattered complaints probably don't carry enough weight to justify reconsidering the policy at this point
The recycling fee has been debated at open city council meetings for several months now without full resolution
Critics raise a fair concern: the flat fee falls hardest on large families with more household waste; the city addresses this by discounting the fee per registered dependent
hints: A real counterargument names the strongest specific objection, not a vague dismissal of 'people who complain.'
Look for the option that grants a true cost is real before explaining how the policy still handles it.

problemText: Draft paragraph addressing the objection that a proposed school dress code limits student self-expression: "That's true, uniforms really would limit how students express themselves, so maybe requiring uniforms isn't worth it after all." Which revision best concedes the true cost and then rebuts it, without abandoning the original claim?
choices: Self-expression through clothing matters a great deal to teenagers, so this really isn't something schools should be interfering with at all
It's true uniforms limit clothing choices; the policy still reduces the visible economic gap between students, a benefit the school judges worth that cost
That's a fair and reasonable point, and it might honestly be reason enough to just drop the uniform proposal altogether
People who support uniform policies are usually just uncomfortable with how teenagers today choose to dress themselves
hints: The draft concedes the cost but then abandons the claim — a rebuttal has to answer the objection, not surrender to it.
Look for the option that grants the real cost AND names a specific reason the position still holds.

problemText: Draft opening for an essay arguing a city should fund a youth job-training program: "This essay will discuss the pros and cons of funding a youth job-training program, a complex issue this city has faced for some time." Which revision most effectively opens the argument by establishing concrete stakes before stating the claim?
choices: Every summer, the unemployment office sees the same graduating seniors return in September, having spent three months applying to jobs that require experience they were never given a chance to build
Youth unemployment is a significant and pressing issue that has affected communities across the entire country for a great many years now
Since the earliest labor markets existed many centuries ago, young workers have struggled to gain their first foothold in the workforce

This essay will discuss, in a balanced and evenhanded way, several considerations relevant to the city's ongoing job-training funding decision, weighing near-term costs against the community's longer-term benefit
hints: A strong opening earns the claim with a concrete, specific scene — not a broad statement about the issue's importance.
Avoid the 'dawn of time' opening and the sentence that just announces the essay's plan.

problemText: Draft conclusion: "In conclusion, this essay has argued that the city should fund the youth job-training program for the reasons stated above, and hopefully readers now agree with this position." Which revision most effectively closes the argument by answering "so what" instead of restating the thesis?
choices: To summarize once more, funding the program is something the city should clearly do given everything already discussed in detail above
As shown throughout this essay, youth job-training matters a great deal, and the reasons given already make the case sufficiently clear
A city that trains its own graduates for its own open jobs stops importing workers it could have grown instead
In closing, this essay has shown that job training is an important issue and that the program deserves the city's continued funding
hints: A strong conclusion projects the claim's significance forward instead of repeating the thesis in the same words.
Test: if you deleted the conclusion, would the essay feel unfinished, or would nothing be lost?
